summaries.example: Imagine you promised to return a friend's library book. A deontologist might say you should keep the promise even if breaking it would be a little more convenient. But this does not mean every duty is absolute. Philosophers ask whether duties can conflict and whether very terrible results could ever change what we should do.
summaries.summary: Deontological ethics is a family of moral theories about what we ought to do. It says that morality is not only a matter of making the best results. Some choices may be forbidden even when they would produce more happiness or save more people. Deontologists also make room for actions that are permitted but not required, so people can care for their families, friends, and own projects. Different versions focus on the agent's intentions or actions, on the rights of people affected, or on rules that people could accept. These theories are attractive because they protect individuals from being sacrificed for a larger goal. They also face difficult questions about conflicting duties, terrible consequences, and how to compare harms to different people.
key_ideas: Deontology says that some actions can be wrong even if they would lead to good results.
It gives an important place to duties, permissions, and rights.
Some deontologists focus on the person acting; others focus on the person affected.
Contractualist views ask what rules people could accept or could not reasonably reject.
Kant is closely connected with deontological ethics because of his ideas about good will, universal rules, and not treating people merely as tools.
summaries.why_it_matters: This way of thinking helps explain why many people believe that good goals do not automatically make every method acceptable. It also helps us notice the moral importance of promises, consent, personal responsibility, and protecting individuals. Studying its problems teaches us that moral decisions can involve more than counting benefits and harms.

important_terms.definition: A kind of moral theory that focuses on duties, rules, rights, and what choices are allowed or forbidden.
A moral theory that judges choices mainly by the results they produce.
Something a person is required to do or not do.
An action that is allowed, even when a person is not required to choose it.
A fair claim that protects a person from certain treatment, such as being used without consent.

questions_to_think_about: Should keeping a promise matter even when breaking it would help more people?
Is there a difference between causing harm and failing to stop harm?
When, if ever, should a very bad result change what a rule requires?
Can two duties ever point in opposite directions?

summaries.example: Consider a runaway trolley that will kill five workers unless it is diverted onto another track where one worker will die. Many people judge switching permissible, while they reject killing one healthy patient to use the patient's organs to save five others. Deontological theories try to explain this difference. A patient-centered view may say the patient is being used as a means in the transplant case, while the one worker is not used in the same way when the trolley is redirected. Agent-centered theories may instead focus on whether the agent intended the death, caused it, or merely redirected an existing threat. These distinctions remain contested.
summaries.summary: Deontological ethics is a family of normative theories that assess choices through duties, rights, permissions, and other norms rather than solely through the states of affairs choices produce. The familiar form gives the Right priority over the Good: certain actions are forbidden even when they would maximize valuable consequences. This priority also creates a space of strong permissions, including choices that need not produce the best outcome, and therefore leaves room for personal commitments and supererogation. Agent-centered theories locate moral significance in the agent's intentions, actions, or causal role. Patient-centered theories explain constraints through rights, especially a prohibition on using another's body, labor, or talents without consent. Contractualist approaches connect wrongness with principles people would accept or could not reasonably reject, though their status as first-order ethics or metaethics is disputed. Kant's views can be interpreted as supporting each strand. Deontology offers a powerful account of why individuals may not be sacrificed for aggregate benefits, but it must address conflicts among duties, the significance of numbers, uncertainty, moral catastrophes, and the risk that detailed exceptions or thresholds make it resemble consequentialism.
key_ideas: Deontology contrasts with consequentialism by giving the Right priority over the Good: some norms constrain action even when violating them would improve outcomes.

Deontological theories differ about the source of moral significance. Agent-centered views emphasize agency, intention, action, or causation; patient-centered views emphasize rights and prohibited use; contractualist views emphasize principles people could accept or could not reasonably reject.

The doctrine of double effect distinguishes intending harm from merely foreseeing or risking it. Related distinctions separate causing from omitting, allowing, enabling, redirecting, or accelerating harm.

A major attraction of deontology is that it protects personal projects and relationships and leaves room for strong permissions and supererogatory acts, meaning actions that are praiseworthy but not required.
Major problems include conflicts among duties, the challenge of explaining how numbers matter, the danger of legalistic rule-avoidance, and cases in which obeying a rule seems to produce catastrophe.

Kant can be associated with all three strands: moral principles and good will support an agent-centered reading, the prohibition on treating people merely as means supports a patient-centered reading, and universalizable maxims support a contractualist reading.
summaries.why_it_matters: Deontological ethics supplies concepts used in debates about rights, consent, responsibility, punishment, promises, and the limits of permissible means. It explains why a person may have a complaint against someone who wrongs them, rather than merely being one unfortunate part of a worse overall outcome. At the same time, its hardest cases show why moral theory cannot stop at a simple rule such as never violate a constraint or always maximize good consequences. The entry presents competing strategies, including absolutist and threshold versions, while leaving their success open to philosophical argument.

important_terms.definition: A normative theory that gives priority to conformity with moral norms, duties, rights, or permissions rather than maximizing valuable outcomes.
The view that the right action is determined by the value of the resulting state of affairs, often by maximizing the Good.
A reason that applies especially to one agent because of that agent's relationships, actions, or responsibilities, rather than equally to everyone.
A deontological approach centered on the agent's intentions, actions, or causal involvement in wrongdoing.
A rights-based approach focused on how a person is treated, especially whether their body, work, or abilities are used without consent.
The idea that a person must not be treated merely as a tool for producing benefits for others without consent.
A view that moral rules govern normally but may be overridden when consequences become extraordinarily disastrous.
The challenge of explaining why violating one moral rule to prevent many similar violations is not always required or permitted.

questions_to_think_about: Can a moral prohibition against harming an innocent person remain binding when violating it would prevent a much greater catastrophe?
Does intending a harm differ morally from foreseeing it, if the outcome and one's control are otherwise the same?
If each person's rights matter equally, why should violating one person's right ever be allowed to prevent several similar violations?
Can a theory preserve deontological constraints without secretly relying on consequentialist calculations?
How should a deontologist reason when it is uncertain whether an action will violate a duty?

summaries.example: Suppose a student finds a lost phone before an important test. Returning it may take time, while keeping it would be easy. A deontologist might say the student's duty not to take someone else's property matters even if keeping the phone brings a small benefit. A consequentialist might ask which choice leads to the best overall result. Deontologists disagree among themselves about why returning it is required: one might focus on the student's action, another on the owner's right, and another on a rule that people could reasonably accept.
summaries.summary: Deontological ethics is a group of theories about what people are morally required, forbidden, or permitted to do. Its main opponent is consequentialism, which judges choices by their results. A deontologist instead holds that some duties or rights place limits on what we may do, even for a good outcome. For example, a person may not be treated as a tool for helping others without consent. Deontologists also allow some choices that are not required, giving people space for family, friendships, and personal goals. There is no single deontological theory. Agent-centered versions focus on intentions, actions, or causation. Patient-centered versions focus on rights and how victims are treated. Contractualist versions ask what rules people could accept. These theories are influential but must explain difficult cases involving numbers, conflicting duties, uncertainty, and terrible consequences.
key_ideas: Deontologists say that some actions are wrong in themselves or wrong because they violate a norm, not simply because they produce bad results.
Consequentialism treats valuable outcomes as central, while deontology treats duties, rights, and permissions as central.
Agent-centered theories focus on the actor's intentions, actions, or causes. Patient-centered theories focus on the people affected and their rights.
The difference between using someone and merely affecting someone helps explain why many people judge a trolley-switch case differently from an organ-transplant case.
Contractualist theories connect morality with principles that people could accept or could not reasonably reject.
Deontology can protect personal relationships and leave room for choices that are good but not required, yet it faces hard cases involving conflicting duties and disastrous consequences.
summaries.why_it_matters: Deontology gives us a way to discuss why methods matter, not only goals. It helps explain everyday judgments about honesty, promises, consent, fairness, and personal responsibility. It also shows why reasonable people can disagree: some focus on intentions, some on rights, and some on rules that everyone could accept. Learning about its weaknesses helps us examine moral rules carefully instead of treating them as automatically simple.

important_terms.definition: An ethical theory that emphasizes duties and rules about what choices are required, forbidden, or allowed.
An ethical theory that judges choices by the value of their consequences.
A requirement to act or avoid acting in a certain way.
A choice that morality allows but does not demand.
A claim or protection that limits how others may treat someone.
A reason that applies specially to one person because of that person's relationships or responsibilities.
A theory focused on how a person is treated, especially whether the person is used to benefit others.
The problem of explaining why violating one rule to stop many similar violations is not always the right choice.

questions_to_think_about: Is breaking a rule acceptable if doing so helps many more people?
Does intending harm make an action worse than merely predicting that harm will happen?
Why might using a person be different from putting that person in danger?
Should morality always tell us to save the larger number?
What should happen when two duties seem to conflict?
